claim: Nonenzymatic replication of RNA is a potential transitional stage between the prebiotic chemistry of nucleotide synthesis and the canonical RNA world in which RNA enzymes (ribozymes) catalyze replication of the RNA genomes of primordial cells.
source: The nonenzymatic replication of RNA is a potential transitional stage between the prebiotic chemistry of nucleotide synthesis and the canonical RNA world in which RNA enzymes (ribozymes) catalyze replication of the RNA genomes of primordial cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about the RNA world hypothesis and the role of nonenzymatic replication as a transitional mechanism.

claim: The plausibility of nonenzymatic RNA replication is undercut by the lack of a protocell-compatible chemical system capable of copying RNA templates containing all four nucleotides.
source: However, the plausibility of nonenzymatic RNA replication is undercut by the lack of a protocell-compatible chemical system capable of copying RNA templates containing all four nucleotides.
evidence: This claim is based on the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study, representing a known limitation.

claim: Short 5′-activated oligonucleotides act as catalysts that accelerate primer extension.
source: We show that short 5′-activated oligonucleotides act as catalysts that accelerate primer extension, and allow for the one-pot copying of mixed sequence RNA templates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Short 5′-activated oligonucleotides allow for the one-pot copying of mixed sequence RNA templates.
source: We show that short 5′-activated oligonucleotides act as catalysts that accelerate primer extension, and allow for the one-pot copying of mixed sequence RNA templates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The fidelity of primer extension products resulting from the sequential addition of activated monomers, when catalyzed by activated oligomers, is sufficient to sustain a genome long enough to encode active ribozymes.
source: The fidelity of the primer extension products resulting from the sequential addition of activated monomers, when catalyzed by activated oligomers, is sufficient to sustain a genome long enough to encode active ribozymes.
evidence: This claim is supported by fidelity measurements presented in Figure 3 and the calculation that 98% fidelity allows for effective genome sizes of 50 nucleotides.

claim: By immobilizing the primer and template on a bead and adding individual monomers in sequence, a significant part of an active hammerhead ribozyme can be synthesized.
source: Finally, by immobilizing the primer and template on a bead and adding individual monomers in sequence, we synthesize a significant part of an active hammerhead ribozyme, forging a link between nonenzymatic polymerization and the RNA world.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The nonenzymatic copying of sequences containing all four nucleotides has not yet been possible for a number of reasons.
source: However, the nonenzymatic copying of sequences containing all four nucleotides has not yet been possible for a number of reasons (Szostak, 2012), most notably the slow rate of primer extension with adenosine and uridine monomers (Joyce et al., 1987; Wu and Orgel, 1992b; Deck et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The slow rate of primer extension with adenosine and uridine monomers is the most notable reason why nonenzymatic copying of sequences containing all four nucleotides has not been possible.
source: However, the nonenzymatic copying of sequences containing all four nucleotides has not yet been possible for a number of reasons (Szostak, 2012), most notably the slow rate of primer extension with adenosine and uridine monomers (Joyce et al., 1987; Wu and Orgel, 1992b; Deck et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Two adjacent A or U residues in the template will stop polymerization entirely under normal conditions.
source: Indeed, two adjacent A or U residues in the template will stop polymerization entirely (Wu and Orgel, 1992b) under normal conditions; even partial copying requires extreme conditions, such as the eutectic phase of frozen samples (Vogel and Richert, 2007), which are not compatible with replication within protocells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Partial copying of templates with adjacent A or U residues requires extreme conditions, such as the eutectic phase of frozen samples.
source: Indeed, two adjacent A or U residues in the template will stop polymerization entirely (Wu and Orgel, 1992b) under normal conditions; even partial copying requires extreme conditions, such as the eutectic phase of frozen samples (Vogel and Richert, 2007), which are not compatible with replication within protocells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The eutectic phase of frozen samples is not compatible with replication within protocells.
source: Indeed, two adjacent A or U residues in the template will stop polymerization entirely (Wu and Orgel, 1992b) under normal conditions; even partial copying requires extreme conditions, such as the eutectic phase of frozen samples (Vogel and Richert, 2007), which are not compatible with replication within protocells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the incompatibility of extreme conditions with protocell environments.

claim: Extensive optimization of reaction conditions improved the rate and regiospecificity of polymerization for G and C but not A and U.
source: Extensive optimization of reaction conditions with the aim of improving the rate of primer extension with all four monomers, including varying the choice of divalent cation and leaving group, improved the rate and regiospecificity of polymerization for G and C but not A and U (Wu and Orgel, 1992b, c; Deck et al., 2011; Inoue and Orgel, 1981; Hagenbuch et al., 2005; Lohrmann et al., 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Low A and U monomer affinity for the template is not the only reason for the slow rate of primer extension with A and U.
source: Recent biophysical studies suggest that low A and U monomer affinity for the template is not the only reason for this problem (Szostak, 2012; Izgu et al., 2015) since A binds only three-fold more weakly than G, but primer extension with A is at least 100-fold slower (Joyce et al., 1987; Wu and Orgel, 1992b; Deck et al., 2011; Heuberger et al., 2015) than with G.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and biophysical studies.

claim: A binds only three-fold more weakly than G to the template.
source: Recent biophysical studies suggest that low A and U monomer affinity for the template is not the only reason for this problem (Szostak, 2012; Izgu et al., 2015) since A binds only three-fold more weakly than G, but primer extension with A is at least 100-fold slower (Joyce et al., 1987; Wu and Orgel, 1992b; Deck et al., 2011; Heuberger et al., 2015) than with G.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous biophysical studies.

claim: Primer extension with A is at least 100-fold slower than with G.
source: Recent biophysical studies suggest that low A and U monomer affinity for the template is not the only reason for this problem (Szostak, 2012; Izgu et al., 2015) since A binds only three-fold more weakly than G, but primer extension with A is at least 100-fold slower (Joyce et al., 1987; Wu and Orgel, 1992b; Deck et al., 2011; Heuberger et al., 2015) than with G.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Downstream helper oligonucleotides provide incoming monomers with an additional binding surface.
source: Moreover, Deck et al. have shown that downstream helper oligonucleotides (Deck et al., 2011) that provide incoming monomers with an additional binding surface improve the binding of A and U monomers, but the underlying difference in rates remains.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Deck et al.

claim: Downstream helper oligonucleotides improve the binding of A and U monomers, but the underlying difference in rates remains.
source: Moreover, Deck et al. have shown that downstream helper oligonucleotides (Deck et al., 2011) that provide incoming monomers with an additional binding surface improve the binding of A and U monomers, but the underlying difference in rates remains.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Deck et al.

claim: The use of helper oligonucleotides allowed primer extension to proceed on a template containing all four bases over the course of several weeks.
source: The use of helper oligonucleotides allowed primer extension to proceed on a template containing all four bases over the course of several weeks, where previously such templates could not be copied at all.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the previous discussion of Deck et al.'s work.

claim: The presence of a leaving group at the 5′ end of a helper oligonucleotide can be a source of significant catalysis.
source: Here we show that the presence of a leaving group at the 5′ end of a helper oligonucleotide can be a source of significant catalysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Activated helper oligonucleotides facilitate the addition of all four RNA monomers individually and in sequence in a single reaction.
source: Activated helper oligonucleotides facilitate the addition of all four RNA monomers individually and in sequence in a single reaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Sequential addition of activated monomers and helper oligonucleotides successfully promoted the synthesis of a significant part of an active hammerhead ribozyme when a template is immobilized by attachment to a bead.
source: Finally, when a template is immobilized by attachment to a bead, sequential addition of activated monomers and helper oligonucleotides successfully promoted the synthesis of a significant part of an active hammerhead ribozyme.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Nucleotides activated with 2-methylimidzole on the 5′-phosphate have been used extensively to model nonenzymatic template copying.
source: Nucleotides activated with 2-methylimidzole on the 5′-phosphate have been used extensively to model nonenzymatic template copying (Deck et al., 2011; Wu and Orgel, 1992c), irrespective of their prebiotic plausibility, and were used in all experiments reported here.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nucleotides activated with 2-methylimidzole on the 5′-phosphate were used in all experiments reported in this study.
source: Nucleotides activated with 2-methylimidzole on the 5′-phosphate have been used extensively to model nonenzymatic template copying (Deck et al., 2011; Wu and Orgel, 1992c), irrespective of their prebiotic plausibility, and were used in all experiments reported here.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experiments conducted in this study.

claim: The primer extension reaction proceeded almost 100 times more rapidly than the ligation reaction.
source: To our surprise, the primer extension reaction proceeded almost 100 times more rapidly than the ligation reaction (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The fully base-paired nicked duplex should be largely in the optimal A-type conformation.
source: We expected the ligation reaction to be faster, because the oligonucleotides to be ligated are both stably bound to the template, and because the fully base-paired nicked duplex should be largely in the optimal A-type conformation (Kozlov and Orgel, 2000), whereas the primer/template complex with template bound monomers would be significantly more disordered.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work and represents established knowledge about RNA structure.

claim: The primer/template complex with template bound monomers would be significantly more disordered than a fully base-paired nicked duplex.
source: We expected the ligation reaction to be faster, because the oligonucleotides to be ligated are both stably bound to the template, and because the fully base-paired nicked duplex should be largely in the optimal A-type conformation (Kozlov and Orgel, 2000), whereas the primer/template complex with template bound monomers would be significantly more disordered.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the structural properties of different RNA complexes.

claim: One of the major differences between monomer addition and ligation is the presence of multiple adjacent 5′-activated nucleotides downstream of the primer in the case of monomer addition, but not ligation.
source: In our search for an explanation for this unexpected observation, we reasoned that one of the major differences between the two scenarios was the presence of multiple adjacent 5′-activated nucleotides downstream of the primer in the case of monomer addition, but not ligation, where there is only a single activated nucleotide.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the experimental design.

claim: Efficient primer extension requires the presence of two activated monomers adjacent to the primer.
source: Furthermore, Orgel et al. showed over 20 years ago that efficient primer extension requires the presence of two activated monomers adjacent to the primer.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to previous work by Orgel et al.

claim: The reaction is fastest when both monomers are activated with 2-methylimidazole instead of either or both being activated with imidazole.
source: Remarkably, the reaction is fastest when both monomers are activated with 2-methylimidazole instead of either or both being activated with imidazole (Wu and Orgel, 1992a), suggesting a possible catalytic role for a physical interaction of the leaving groups of adjacent monomers.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Wu and Orgel.

claim: There is a possible catalytic role for a physical interaction of the leaving groups of adjacent monomers.
source: Remarkably, the reaction is fastest when both monomers are activated with 2-methylimidazole instead of either or both being activated with imidazole (Wu and Orgel, 1992a), suggesting a possible catalytic role for a physical interaction of the leaving groups of adjacent monomers.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observation about 2-methylimidazole activation.

claim: Primer extension by addition of a single monomer, in the absence of any additional downstream mono- or oligo-nucleotides, was very slow and comparable in rate to the ligation of the primer to a 5′-activated GAG trinucleotide.
source: Primer extension by addition of a single monomer, in the absence of any additional downstream mono- or oligo-nucleotides, was very slow and comparable in rate to the ligation of the primer to a 5′-activated GAG trinucleotide (Figure 1c–f, reactions 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c-f.

claim: The binding of an unactivated AGC trimer, with either a 5′ hydroxyl or a 5′ phosphate, downstream of an activated G monomer conferred only a modest increase in the rate of addition of the G monomer to the primer.
source: The binding of an unactivated AGC trimer, with either a 5′ hydroxyl or a 5′ phosphate, downstream of an activated G monomer conferred only a modest increase in the rate of addition of the G monomer to the primer (Figure 1c–f, reactions 4 and 5), consistent with previous reports of unactivated downstream 'helper' oligonucleotides (Deck et al., 2011; Jauker et al., 2015; Kervio et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c-f and citations to previous literature.

claim: Unactivated helper oligonucleotides are thought to act largely by increasing monomer affinity to the primer/template complex by providing an additional base-stacking surface.
source: Such helper oligonucleotides are thought to act largely by increasing monomer affinity to the primer/template complex by providing an additional base-stacking surface.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about the mechanism of helper oligonucleotides.

claim: When the AGC trimer was activated as a 5′-phosphoro-2-methylimidazolide and used as a downstream helper oligonucleotide, the rate of primer extension was increased by over two orders of magnitude compared to reactions with unactivated trimers.
source: In contrast, when the same AGC trimer was activated as a 5′-phosphoro-2-methylimidazolide and used as a downstream helper oligonucleotide, the rate of primer extension (by addition of a G monomer) was increased by over two orders of magnitude (Figure 1c–f, reaction 6) compared to reactions with unactivated trimers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c-f.

claim: The rate of primer extension with a single G in the presence of an activated downstream trinucleotide was about twice as fast as the rate when the primer was followed by up to four sequential activated G monomers.
source: The rate of primer extension with a single G in the presence of an activated downstream trinucleotide was about twice as fast as the rate when the primer was followed by up to four sequential activated G monomers (Figure 1c–f, reaction 1 and 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c-f.

claim: At saturating concentrations of each of the oligonucleotides, the rate of primer extension improved as the length of the helper increased from mononucleotide to dinucleotide to trinucleotide, and then stayed approximately constant with the tetranucleotide.
source: At saturating concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) of each of the oligonucleotides, the rate of primer extension improved as the length of the helper increased from mononucleotide to dinucleotide to trinucleotide, and then stayed approximately constant with the tetranucleotide (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At subsaturating concentrations of helper oligonucleotide, the rate of the primer extension reaction increased with increasing concentrations of di- or tri-nucleotide helper.
source: At subsaturating concentrations of helper oligonucleotide, the rate of the primer extension reaction increased with increasing concentrations of di- or tri-nucleotide helper (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The maximum rate of the trimer-assisted reaction was significantly faster than that of the dimer-assisted reaction.
source: Because the maximum rate of the trimer-assisted reaction was significantly faster than that of the dimer-assisted reaction, we proceeded with trimers as the downstream helper oligonucleotides for the remainder of this study.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rate of primer extension increased by at least two orders of magnitude for all four monomers (A, G, C and U) when assisted by a downstream 2-methylimidazole-activated AGC trimer compared to reactions without any helper oligonucleotides.
source: In each case, the rate of primer extension increased by at least two orders of magnitude compared to the corresponding reactions without any helper oligonucleotides (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The rate of primer extension with A and U monomers was previously too slow to measure, conservatively estimated to be at least three orders of magnitude slower than primer extension with G or C monomers.
source: Remarkably, whereas the rate of primer extension with A and U monomers was previously too slow to measure (Wu and Orgel, 1992b; Heuberger et al., 2015) – conservatively estimated to be at least three orders of magnitude slower than primer extension with G or C monomers – the difference in polymerization rates was reduced to roughly one order of magnitude when assisted by downstream activated trimers (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The difference in polymerization rates between A/U and G/C monomers was reduced to roughly one order of magnitude when assisted by downstream activated trimers.
source: Remarkably, whereas the rate of primer extension with A and U monomers was previously too slow to measure (Wu and Orgel, 1992b; Heuberger et al., 2015) – conservatively estimated to be at least three orders of magnitude slower than primer extension with G or C monomers – the difference in polymerization rates was reduced to roughly one order of magnitude when assisted by downstream activated trimers (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The overall fidelity of trimer-assisted polymerization is 98%.
source: By averaging the fidelities of the four templates we found the overall fidelity of trimer-assisted polymerization to be 98%.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Assuming an error threshold of one mutation per genome, a fidelity of 98% allows for effective genome sizes of 50 nucleotides.
source: Assuming an error threshold of one mutation per genome (Eigen, 1971), this value of fidelity allows for effective genome sizes of 50 nucleotides, long enough to produce functional ribozymes (Ferré-D'Amaré and Scott, 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on a calculation using the measured fidelity and citations to previous work on error thresholds and ribozyme sizes.

claim: Genome sizes of 50 nucleotides are long enough to produce functional ribozymes.
source: Assuming an error threshold of one mutation per genome (Eigen, 1971), this value of fidelity allows for effective genome sizes of 50 nucleotides, long enough to produce functional ribozymes (Ferré-D'Amaré and Scott, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on ribozyme sizes.

claim: The fastest mismatch reaction was primer extension by G during copying of a template U, which was approximately 5% as fast as primer extension with A on the same template.
source: The fastest mismatch reaction was primer extension by G during copying of a template U, which was approximately 5% as fast as primer extension with A on the same template (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The G:U mismatch is likely due to the formation of a G:U wobble base pair.
source: This is likely due to the formation of a G:U wobble base pair (Heuberger et al., 2015), and is consistent with previous studies of nonenzymatic primer extension reactions (Rajamani et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on inference supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: All mismatches other than G:U were at least two orders of magnitude slower than their matched counterparts.
source: All other mismatches were at least two orders of magnitude slower than their matched counterparts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Replacing the canonical U monomer with 2-thiouridine and 2-thioribothymine improved the polymerization rates by approximately one order of magnitude.
source: We also tested the effect of replacing the canonical U monomer with 2-thiouridine and 2-thioribothymine on the polymerization rate and found, in line with previous reports (Heuberger et al., 2015), that this sulfur substitution improved the rates by approximately one order of magnitude (Figure 3b), bringing the rate of primer extension closer to the rates of G and C addition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and a citation to previous work.

claim: Sulfur substitution in U monomers brings the rate of primer extension closer to the rates of G and C addition.
source: We also tested the effect of replacing the canonical U monomer with 2-thiouridine and 2-thioribothymine on the polymerization rate and found, in line with previous reports (Heuberger et al., 2015), that this sulfur substitution improved the rates by approximately one order of magnitude (Figure 3b), bringing the rate of primer extension closer to the rates of G and C addition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: After a downstream activated trimer catalyzes the addition of the first monomer to the primer, the helper trimer must dissociate to allow for the binding of the next monomer-trimer pair.
source: In order to iterate the process of trimer assisted monomer addition, after a downstream activated trimer catalyzes the addition of the first monomer to the primer, the helper trimer must dissociate to allow for the binding of the next monomer-trimer pair.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the mechanism of iterative primer extension.

claim: In the absence of activated trimers, almost no primer extension was observed even though all four monomers were present.
source: In the absence of activated trimers, we observed almost no primer extension (lane 1 Figure 4b); even though all four monomers were present, their combined rate of addition was not measurable.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Adding just the first helper trimer resulted in rapid addition of the first monomer (C) to the primer, followed by slow addition of the first trimer (AGC) to the growing primer.
source: Adding just the first helper trimer resulted in rapid addition of the first monomer (C) to the primer, followed by slow addition of the first trimer (AGC) to the growing primer.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Adding two, three or four trimers together resulted in the generation of primers extended by two, three or four monomers respectively.
source: Similarly, adding two, three or four trimers together resulted in the generation of primers extended by two, three or four monomers respectively (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Reactions with all four trimers converted primer into a product with four sequentially added monomers with an ~80% yield after 16 hr.
source: These reactions converted primer into a product with four sequentially added monomers with an ~80% yield after 16 hr (Figure 4c,d); single monomer addition reactions reached >95% yield after only 10 min (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c,d.

claim: Single monomer addition reactions reached >95% yield after only 10 min.
source: These reactions converted primer into a product with four sequentially added monomers with an ~80% yield after 16 hr (Figure 4c,d); single monomer addition reactions reached >95% yield after only 10 min (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The difference between the fast rates observed in the trimer-assisted addition of a single base and the slower rate of trimer-assisted polymerization of all four bases simultaneously may be due to the competition of trimers for overlapping binding sites on the template.
source: The difference between the fast rates observed in the trimer-assisted addition of a single base (Figure 2b) and the slower rate of trimer-assisted polymerization of all four bases simultaneously (Figure 4b) may be due to the competition of trimers for overlapping binding sites on the template.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The hypothesis that competition of trimers for overlapping binding sites slows polymerization is supported by the decreased rate of trimer assisted primer extension with a single monomer in the presence of additional overlapping downstream trimers.
source: This hypothesis is supported by the decreased rate of trimer assisted primer extension with a single monomer in the presence of additional overlapping downstream trimers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The copying of templates containing two consecutive A or U monomers is made possible by the use of activated helper oligonucleotides.
source: The copying of templates containing two consecutive A or U monomers is also made possible by the use of activated helper oligonucleotides (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: A high conversion rate (75–95%) was observed at each step of the sequential monomer addition on beads.
source: Primer extension was monitored by gel electrophoresis. Despite the fact that no 2-thiouridine monomers were used (in order to protect the catalytic capacity of the ribozyme) a high conversion rate was observed at each step (75–95%) (Figure 6b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The reaction durations required to achieve high conversion rates varied widely in the bead-based synthesis.
source: The reaction durations required to achieve these conversion rates varied widely, for example, the seventh monomer addition required 21 hr to reach 95% while the eighth addition reached the same level of conversion after just 30 min.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Generally, G and C additions were much faster than A or U additions in the bead-based synthesis.
source: Generally, G and C additions were much faster than A or U additions; the reason for the discrepancy between the rates of these reactions on beads and those in solution is unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The reason for the discrepancy between the rates of reactions on beads and those in solution is unknown.
source: Generally, G and C additions were much faster than A or U additions; the reason for the discrepancy between the rates of these reactions on beads and those in solution is unknown.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of lack of knowledge about the mechanism.

claim: Despite the crude reaction product with full-length HH2 comprising only 6% of the reaction products, the product mixture was able to function as a catalyst, with 50% ribozyme cleavage yield.
source: Despite the fact that this was a crude reaction product, with full-length HH2 comprising only 6% of the reaction products, the product mixture was able to function as a catalyst, with 50% ribozyme cleavage yield, thus demonstrating that a significant portion of an active ribozyme was synthesized nonenzymatically.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: A significant portion of an active ribozyme was synthesized nonenzymatically.
source: Despite the fact that this was a crude reaction product, with full-length HH2 comprising only 6% of the reaction products, the product mixture was able to function as a catalyst, with 50% ribozyme cleavage yield, thus demonstrating that a significant portion of an active ribozyme was synthesized nonenzymatically.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Short activated oligonucleotides are plausibly generated by either templated or untemplated monomer polymerization.
source: Short, activated oligonucleotides – themselves plausibly generated by either templated or untemplated monomer polymerization – are efficient catalysts of high fidelity primer extension with all four RNA monomers.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on reasoning about plausible prebiotic chemistry.

claim: Short activated oligonucleotides are efficient catalysts of high fidelity primer extension with all four RNA monomers.
source: Short, activated oligonucleotides – themselves plausibly generated by either templated or untemplated monomer polymerization – are efficient catalysts of high fidelity primer extension with all four RNA monomers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Short activated oligonucleotides can play dual roles, acting either as catalysts of chain growth by monomer addition, or directly as replication intermediates, since they can also be incorporated into a growing chain by ligation.
source: Thus short activated oligonucleotides can play dual roles, acting either as catalysts of chain growth by monomer addition, or directly as replication intermediates, since they can also be incorporated into a growing chain by ligation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental observations about both catalysis and ligation.

claim: Template copying in a complex but realistic milieu containing both activated monomers and oligomers could occur via a hybrid process combining primer extension with monomers and oligonucleotide ligation.
source: Template copying in a complex but realistic milieu containing both activated monomers and oligomers could therefore occur via a hybrid process combining primer extension with monomers and oligonucleotide ligation.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The disparity in rates between the reactions catalyzed by activated vs. unactivated trimers indicates a key role for the leaving group downstream of the polymerizing monomer.
source: The disparity in rates between the reactions catalyzed by activated vs. unactivated trimers indicates a key role for the leaving group downstream of the polymerizing monomer.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data comparing activated and unactivated trimers.

claim: The slow rate of activated oligonucleotide ligation is explained by the lack of a leaving group one base downstream of the site of the primer extension reaction.
source: The slow rate of activated oligonucleotide ligation is also explained by the lack of a leaving group one base downstream of the site of the primer extension reaction: in this case the downstream position corresponds to the second monomer in the oligonucleotide which necessarily has no leaving group as it is linked to the upstream monomer by a phosphodiester linkage.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the structural differences between ligation and polymerization reactions.

claim: The nature of the interaction between the downstream leaving group and the reacting monomer remains unclear.
source: The nature of the interaction between the downstream leaving group and the reacting monomer remains unclear.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of lack of knowledge about the mechanism.

claim: It is possible that the downstream leaving group interacts attractively with the reacting leaving group, positioning it optimally for attack by the 3′ hydroxyl of the primer.
source: It is possible that the downstream leaving group interacts attractively with the reacting leaving group, positioning it optimally for attack by the 3′ hydroxyl of the primer.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism.

claim: Wu et al. observed that the interaction between leaving groups could be very sensitive to steric effects, such that 2-methylimidazole at the downstream position would facilitate polymerization much more effectively than imidazole.
source: As observed by Wu et al. (Wu and Orgel, 1992a) this interaction could be very sensitive to steric effects, such that 2-methylimidazole at the downstream position would facilitate polymerization much more effectively than imidazole, though the authors ultimately concluded that such subtle effects are not likely to adequately explain the strength of the interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Wu et al.

claim: Wu et al. ultimately concluded that subtle steric effects are not likely to adequately explain the strength of the interaction between leaving groups.
source: As observed by Wu et al. (Wu and Orgel, 1992a) this interaction could be very sensitive to steric effects, such that 2-methylimidazole at the downstream position would facilitate polymerization much more effectively than imidazole, though the authors ultimately concluded that such subtle effects are not likely to adequately explain the strength of the interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Wu et al.

claim: Wu et al. suggested that the catalytic effect could be due to acid-base catalysis.
source: Wu et al. (Wu and Orgel, 1992a) also suggested that the catalytic effect could be due to acid-base catalysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Wu et al.

claim: Another possibility is that the upstream leaving group forms a covalent bond with the phosphate of the downstream monomer, a reaction that is only possible if there is a leaving group on the downstream monomer.
source: Another possibility is that the upstream leaving group forms a covalent bond with the phosphate of the downstream monomer, a reaction that is only possible if there is a leaving group on the downstream monomer (Kervio et al., 2016 and T. Walton and J.W. Szostak, unpublished data).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism supported by a citation and unpublished data.

claim: The covalent bond between leaving groups could form before the attack of the 3′ hydroxyl of the primer, creating an imidazolium intermediate, or in a concerted reaction where the leaving group of the upstream monomer replaces the leaving group of the downstream monomer.
source: This covalent bond could form before the attack of the 3′ hydroxyl of the primer, creating an imidazolium intermediate, or in a concerted reaction where the leaving group of the upstream monomer replaces the leaving group of the downstream monomer.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing possible reaction mechanisms.

claim: Further understanding of the reaction mechanism could lead to concomitant improvements in the rate and extent of template copying.
source: Further understanding of the reaction mechanism could lead to concomitant improvements in the rate and extent of template copying.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing potential future improvements.

claim: The copying of long mixed template sequences under the conditions described compares favorably, both in terms of rate and efficiency with reactions in which arbitrary RNA templates are copied by highly evolved ribozyme polymerases.
source: However, the copying of long mixed template sequences under our conditions compares favorably, both in terms of rate and efficiency with reactions in which arbitrary RNA templates are copied by highly evolved ribozyme polymerases (Wochner et al., 2011) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with cited previous work and data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: If the rates and fidelities of nonenzymatic RNA polymerization were sufficiently high, the need for a ribozyme polymerase in the RNA world may be circumvented.
source: In fact, if the rates and fidelities of nonenzymatic RNA polymerization were sufficiently high, the need for a ribozyme polymerase in the RNA world may be circumvented: RNA could be copied by nonenzymatic chemistry alone until the advent of protein polymerases.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible scenario for the RNA world.

claim: RNA could be copied by nonenzymatic chemistry alone until the advent of protein polymerases if the rates and fidelities of nonenzymatic RNA polymerization were sufficiently high.
source: In fact, if the rates and fidelities of nonenzymatic RNA polymerization were sufficiently high, the need for a ribozyme polymerase in the RNA world may be circumvented: RNA could be copied by nonenzymatic chemistry alone until the advent of protein polymerases.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible scenario for the RNA world.

claim: The identification of a plausible source of chemical energy that could drive the re-activation of monomers and oligomers following hydrolytic loss of the leaving group is a key missing component in efforts to reconstitute nonenzymatic RNA replication.
source: We suggest that the identification of a plausible source of chemical energy that could drive the re-activation of monomers and oligomers following hydrolytic loss of the leaving group is a key missing component in efforts to reconstitute nonenzymatic RNA replication.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' opinion about what is needed for future progress.

claim: A chemical environment that could maintain a fully activated pool of substrates, and avoid accumulation of the inhibitory by-products resulting from hydrolysis, might be sufficient to drive high yielding and complete copying of longer RNA templates in one pot.
source: A chemical environment that could maintain a fully activated pool of substrates, and avoid accumulation of the inhibitory by-products resulting from hydrolysis, might be sufficient to drive high yielding and complete copying of longer RNA templates in one pot, thus setting the stage for the emergence of Darwinian evolution.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing what might be sufficient for future progress.

claim: Maintaining a fully activated pool of substrates and avoiding accumulation of inhibitory by-products could set the stage for the emergence of Darwinian evolution.
source: A chemical environment that could maintain a fully activated pool of substrates, and avoid accumulation of the inhibitory by-products resulting from hydrolysis, might be sufficient to drive high yielding and complete copying of longer RNA templates in one pot, thus setting the stage for the emergence of Darwinian evolution.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a connection between improved replication and the emergence of evolution.

claim: The final yield of the +12 product in the bead-assisted synthesis was 6%.
source: Final yield of the +12 product was 6%.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 6.

claim: The total time required for the bead-assisted synthesis of 12 nucleotides was 150 hr.
source: Steps varied in length from 30 min to 22 hr; the total time required was 150 hr.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 6.

claim: Primer extension reactions can reach yields greater than 7 nucleotides in one pot, but only in low yields.
source: While our method can only produce sequences >7 nucleotides in one reaction in low yields (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) due to the cross-inhibitory effect of trimers with overlapping binding sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), we reasoned that a ribozyme could be synthesized by this approach if monomers were added, along with their attendant trimers, one at a time (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.
